Dravidian Much of English is made up of words from other languages, và Dravidian, a group of languages spoken in southern India và northeastern Sri Lanka, including Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, và Malayalam, is a small but significant contributor in this respect. From southern South Asia English has received especially names for foods, plants và materials from plants, và terms of music và dance.

From the cuisine of the region have come curry (late 16th century, from Tamil ka?i "sauce"), dosa (a pancake, from Tamil), mango (late 16th, via Portuguese và Malay from Tamil), mulligatawny (late 18th, from Tamil mi?aku-ta??i "pepper-water"), poppadom (early 19th, from Tamil), và sambhar (a spiced vegetarian stew, mid-20th, via Tamil from Sanskrit sambhara "collection"). Malayalam has given people the cachou to sweeten the breath (late 16th century, via French) và the jak fruit (late 16th, via Portuguese).

Names of plants và their products include areca (late 16th century, via Portuguese from Malayalam), betel (mid-16th, via Portuguese from Malayalam ve??ila, itself from Tamil), coir (coconut fiber, late 16th, from Malayalam), copra (dried coconut, late 16th, from Malayalam via Portuguese), patchouli, source of an aromatic oil (mid-19th, from Tamil), poon (late 17th, via Sinhalese from Malayalam hoặc Tamil), teak (late 17th, via Portuguese from Tamil hoặc Malayalam tekku), và vetiver (mid-19th, via French from Tamil ve??iver, from ver "root"). Migrating animals include the bandicoot (late 18th, from Telugu pandikokku, literally "pig-rat") và the dhole (a wild dog, early 19th, probably from Kannada to?a "wolf").

In the arts have come Kathakali, a form of drama combining dance và mime (from a Malayalam compound formed from Sanskrit katha "story" + Malayalam ka?i "play"), mridanga, a kind of drum (from Tamil), và perhaps the tom-tom (from an imitative form in either Telugu hoặc Hindi). A migrant with an unexpected musical connection is pariah: hereditary drummers in southern India belonged to a low caste, và the word comes from Tamil pa?aiyan "drummer."

Some of the less obvious Dravidian migrants fall into no particular category: catamaran (early 17th century, from Tamil ka??umaram "tied wood"), cheroot (late 17th, via French from Tamil), cot (mid-17th, from Hindi kha? "framework strung with rope và used as a bed," via Sanskrit from Tamil ka??u "tie"), và godown ("warehouse," late 16th), which looks like a word formed from English elements but in fact came via Portuguese gudao from Tamil kitanku, Kannada gadangu "store."
